books.name: The Constitution
books.sub: How the rule book was written and how it works

stories.title: The borrowed bag
stories.teaser: The makers read sixty constitutions and took the best of each.
body: In 1947 a group of lawyers sat down in Delhi to write a rule book for a new country. They did not start with an empty page. **B. N. Rau**, the adviser to the Constituent Assembly, had studied the constitutions of about sixty countries. Dr Ambedkar was not shy about this. He said nobody owns good ideas, so there is no shame in borrowing them.
The biggest loan came from home. The **Government of India Act, 1935** gave the federal plan, the office of Governor, the Public Service Commissions and the emergency rules.

From **Britain** came the parliamentary system, the rule of law, the writs and **single citizenship**. From the **USA** came the Fundamental Rights, judicial review and the impeachment of the President.

**Ireland** gave three things: the Directive Principles, the way the President is elected, and the **nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha**. **Canada** gave a federation with a strong Centre, and the rule that left-over (residuary) powers go to the Centre. **Australia** gave the **Concurrent List** and the joint sitting of the two Houses.

Then come the small loans that examiners love. The idea of **suspending Fundamental Rights during an Emergency** came from the **Weimar Constitution of Germany**. The **Fundamental Duties** came from the **USSR**. The way to amend the Constitution came from **South Africa**. “Procedure established by law” came from **Japan**. Liberty, equality and fraternity came from **France**.
The exam has already asked Britain (2021) and Ireland (2025). The next country on the list is waiting.
keep: Emergency suspension of rights: Germany (Weimar).
Rajya Sabha nominations, Directive Principles, election of President: Ireland.
Concurrent List, joint sitting: Australia.
Residuary powers with the Centre: Canada.
Fundamental Duties: USSR. Amendment procedure: South Africa.

stories.title: The page before page one
stories.teaser: Is the Preamble a part of the Constitution? The judges took thirteen years to agree.
body: On 13 December 1946 Jawaharlal Nehru stood up in the Constituent Assembly and moved the **Objectives Resolution**. It said what kind of country India wished to be. Three years later that speech had become one long sentence, the Preamble. It was adopted with the rest of the Constitution on **26 November 1949**.

The sentence begins with “We, the people of India”. It calls India a **Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic**. Then it promises four things in a fixed order: **Justice** (social, economic and political), **Liberty** (of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship), **Equality** (of status and of opportunity) and **Fraternity**.

But is this page really a part of the book? In the **Berubari Union case (1960)** the Supreme Court said no. In the **Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)** the Court changed its mind and said yes. Parliament can amend the Preamble, but it cannot destroy the basic features.
Parliament has amended it **only once**. The **42nd Amendment (1976)** added three words: **Socialist, Secular and Integrity**.
One more point is a favourite trap. The Preamble **cannot be enforced in a court**. You cannot file a case saying “the Preamble promised me justice”.

Great men gave it names. Ernest Barker called it the **key-note** of the Constitution. K. M. Munshi called it the **horoscope** of the republic. Thakurdas Bhargava called it the **soul**. N. A. Palkhivala called it the **identity card**.
keep: Berubari 1960: not a part. Kesavananda Bharati 1973: a part.
Amended once: 42nd Amendment, 1976 (Socialist, Secular, Integrity).
Not enforceable in court.
Key-note: Barker. Horoscope: Munshi. Soul: Bhargava. Identity card: Palkhivala.

asked.q:
Consider the following statements about the Preamble:
1. In the Berubari Union case (1960), the Supreme Court said the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution.
2. In the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Supreme Court said the Preamble is a part of the Constitution.
3. The Preamble has been amended only once so far.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

stories.title: Six rights and five keys
stories.teaser: Some rights belong to every person in India. Five belong only to citizens.
body: Part III of the Constitution, **Articles 12 to 35**, holds the Fundamental Rights. Think of them as six rooms: equality (14–18), freedom (19–22), protection from exploitation (23–24), religion (**25–28**), culture and education (29–30), and the right to go to court (32).

A foreign tourist in Puri also has rights. The police cannot treat her unequally (Article 14) or take her life or liberty without law (Article 21). But five Articles are kept **only for citizens: 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30**. So the six freedoms of **Article 19**, such as free speech and the freedom to move anywhere in India, are not for foreigners.

**Article 21** is the smallest Article with the biggest family. The courts keep reading new rights into the words “life and personal liberty”. The right to **privacy** came in 2017 from a nine-judge bench (asked in 2018). **Maternity leave** came in 2025 (asked in 2025). In January 2026 the Court added **menstrual health** ⟨CHECK⟩. Education has its own number, **21A**, added by the 86th Amendment.

A right is useless without a way to enforce it. That way is **Article 32**, which Dr Ambedkar called the heart and soul of the Constitution. The Supreme Court (Article 32) and the High Courts (Article 226) use five writs, like five keys.

**Habeas Corpus** frees a person held illegally. **Mandamus** orders an official to do his duty. **Prohibition** stops a lower court in the middle of a case. **Certiorari** cancels an order a lower court has already passed. **Quo Warranto** asks a person, “By what authority do you hold this public office?”
keep: Citizens only: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, 30.
Article 21: privacy, maternity leave, menstrual health (check the last one).
Religion: Articles 25 to 28. Education: 21A.
Quo Warranto questions a person’s claim to a public office.
Mandamus was asked in 2018; Prohibition and Quo Warranto are next.

asked.q: Which writ is issued by a court to ask a person by what authority he or she holds a public office?
Which of the following Fundamental Rights is available only to citizens of India and not to foreigners?
In January 2026 the Supreme Court held that menstrual health and hygiene is a part of the right to life and dignity. This right flows from:

stories.title: Promises and drawers
stories.teaser: Learn the Directive Principles by number and the Schedules by what is inside.
body: Part IV, **Articles 36 to 51**, is a list of promises the State makes to itself. These are the Directive Principles, an idea taken from Ireland. No court can enforce them, but a government is judged by them.

The exam now asks them by number. Walk down the corridor once. **39A** is free legal aid, added in 1976. **40** is village panchayats. **44** is a uniform civil code. **45** is care of young children. **47** is nutrition and the ban on harmful drinks. **48** is farming and cow protection. **48A** is the environment. **50** asks the State to **separate the judiciary from the executive**. **51** is about international peace, which is why it is called the Article on foreign policy.
In 2025 the paper asked Article 51 and gave Article 50 as a wrong option. Wrong options often become next year’s answers.

At the back of the book are the **twelve Schedules**. Think of them as twelve drawers. The **First** has the names of States and Union Territories. The **Second** has salaries. The **Third** has the **forms of oaths**. The **Fourth** has the seats of each State in the Rajya Sabha. The **Fifth** is for Scheduled Areas and the **Sixth** for the tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

The **Seventh** has the three lists: Union, State and Concurrent. The **Eighth** has the 22 languages. The **Ninth**, added by the very first amendment in 1951, protects certain laws from the courts. The **Tenth** is the anti-defection law. The **Eleventh** lists 29 subjects for Panchayats and the **Twelfth** lists 18 subjects for Municipalities.
The 2025 paper put oaths in the Second drawer to trick you. They live in the Third.
keep: Article 50: separate judiciary from executive. Article 51: foreign policy.
Article 39A: free legal aid (1976). Article 40: panchayats. Article 44: uniform civil code.
Second Schedule: salaries. Third: oaths. Fourth: Rajya Sabha seats.
Ninth Schedule came with the 1st Amendment, 1951.
Eleventh: 29 subjects. Twelfth: 18 subjects.

asked.q: Which Article of the Constitution asks the State to separate the judiciary from the executive?
Which Schedule of the Constitution contains the forms of oaths and affirmations?

stories.title: A book that keeps changing
stories.teaser: The amendments the examiner returns to, and one change that is not an amendment at all.
body: The Constitution has a door for change, **Article 368**. More than a hundred amendments have walked through it. The examiner keeps coming back to about a dozen.

The **1st (1951)** added the Ninth Schedule. The **42nd (1976)**, passed during the Emergency, was so large that people call it a mini-constitution. It added three words to the Preamble, the Fundamental Duties and free legal aid, and it moved **education** from the State List to the Concurrent List. The **44th (1978)** undid some of the damage. It removed the right to property from the Fundamental Rights and replaced “internal disturbance” with “armed rebellion” as a ground for Emergency.

The **52nd (1985)** brought the anti-defection law. The **61st (1988)** lowered the **voting age from 21 to 18**. The **69th (1991)** made Delhi the National Capital Territory. The **73rd and 74th (1992)** gave Panchayats and Municipalities a place in the Constitution; both took effect in 1993.

The **86th (2002)** made education a right. The **91st (2003)** capped the Council of Ministers at **15%** of the Lok Sabha. The **99th** set up a commission to appoint judges; it came into force in 2015 and the Supreme Court struck it down the same year. The **101st (2016)** brought GST, the **103rd (2019)** the 10% quota for the poor among the general category, and the **106th (2023)** one-third seats for women.

Now the twist. In 2026 Kerala became **Keralam**. That was not done through Article 368. Under **Article 3**, Parliament can create a State or change its area, boundary or **name** by an ordinary law. The President must recommend the Bill and must first send it to the State Legislature for its views. Those views are not binding. **Article 4** says such a law is not counted as an amendment. Orissa became Odisha in 2011.
keep: 61st Amendment (1988): voting age 21 to 18.
42nd: Socialist, Secular, Integrity; Fundamental Duties. 44th: property right removed.
69th: Delhi NCT. 91st: ministers capped at 15%. 99th: in force 2015.
Renaming a State: Article 3, ordinary law, not Article 368.

asked.q: The name of Kerala was changed to 'Keralam' in 2026. Under which Article can Parliament change the name of a State by an ordinary law?

stories.title: Follow the rupee
stories.teaser: From the budget speech to the auditor’s report, every rupee walks a fixed road.
body: Every year the Finance Minister reads the budget. The Constitution calls it the **Annual Financial Statement (Article 112)**. Follow one rupee from that speech.

To raise or spend that rupee, the government needs a **Money Bill**, defined in **Article 110**. A Money Bill can start only in the **Lok Sabha**, and only with the President’s recommendation. If there is a doubt, the **Speaker** decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill, and that decision is final.
The Rajya Sabha gets the Bill for just **14 days**. It can only suggest changes. The Lok Sabha **may accept or reject** them (asked in 2025). There is no joint sitting on a Money Bill.

The budget takes weeks to pass, but salaries cannot wait. So Parliament gives an advance called a **Vote on Account** (asked in 2018). Members who want to protest move cut motions. A **policy cut** reduces a demand to **₹1**. A **token cut** reduces it by **₹100**.

After the rupee is spent, one man checks the bills: the **Comptroller and Auditor General**. The **President appoints** him (asked in 2021) under **Article 148**. He serves **six years or till the age of 65**. He gives his reports to the President, who places them before Parliament.

There the **Public Accounts Committee** reads them. It has **22 members**, 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha, and its chairman usually comes from the Opposition. Because the committee leans on the auditor at every step, the CAG is called its **friend, philosopher and guide**. The present CAG is **K. Sanjay Murthy**.
keep: Money Bill: Article 110, Lok Sabha only, Speaker certifies.
Rajya Sabha has 14 days; Lok Sabha may accept or reject.
CAG: Article 148, appointed by the President, six years or 65.
CAG is the friend, philosopher and guide of the Public Accounts Committee (22 members).
Vote on Account: advance grant before the budget is passed.

stories.title: The view from Bhubaneswar
stories.teaser: The Governor, the one House Odisha has, and the ladder of ages.
body: Stand outside the Raj Bhavan in Bhubaneswar. The person inside, the **Governor**, was not elected by anyone in Odisha. The **President appoints** the Governor (Article 155), and the Governor stays only **during the pleasure of the President** (Article 156). There is **no impeachment** of a Governor. The State Assembly cannot remove him.

A Governor must be **35 years** old. Since the 7th Amendment of 1956, **one person can be Governor of two or more States**. In 2025 the paper asked who wanted Governors to be non-partisan people from outside the State’s politics. That was the **Sarkaria Commission**. In October 2026 **Braj Mohan Ram** was named Governor of Odisha, after Hari Babu Kambhampati.

Now walk to the Assembly. Odisha has only one House. Just **six States** have a second House, the Legislative Council: **Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra and Karnataka**. Odisha’s Assembly asked for one in 2018, but Parliament has not created it.

That is the rule of **Article 169**. The Assembly passes a resolution by a special majority, and then **Parliament** creates or abolishes the Council by an ordinary law (asked in 2021). A Council can have at most one-third of the Assembly’s strength and at least 40 members.

Last, the ladder of ages. You vote at **18**. You can sit in a Panchayat or Municipality at **21**. You can enter the Lok Sabha or an Assembly at **25**. The Rajya Sabha and a Legislative Council need **30** (asked in 2025). The President, the Vice-President and a Governor need **35**.
keep: Governor: appointed and removed by the President; no impeachment; age 35.
One person can be Governor of two or more States (7th Amendment).
Six States have a Council; Odisha does not.
Council is created or abolished by Parliament under Article 169.
Ages: 18 vote, 21 Panchayat, 25 Lok Sabha, 30 Rajya Sabha and Council, 35 Governor.

stories.title: The watchdogs
stories.teaser: The Commission that will conduct your exam, and the one that guards human rights.
body: The body that will hold your exam, the OPSC, is written into the Constitution itself. **Articles 315 to 323** set up the Union and State Public Service Commissions.

The **Governor appoints** the chairman and members of a State Commission. Yet the Governor cannot remove them. **Only the President** can, after an inquiry by the Supreme Court. The makers did this so that no State government could frighten the people who select its officers.

A member serves **six years**. In the **UPSC** the age limit is **65**. In a **State Commission** it is **62**. Two or more States can share a **Joint Commission**, and that is created by **Parliament** (asked in 2025). After leaving, the UPSC chairman can take no further government job (asked in 2021).

The second watchdog is younger. The **National Human Rights Commission** is not in the Constitution. It was set up under the **Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993**. Its first chairperson was **Justice Ranganath Misra** (asked in 2021).

At first only a former Chief Justice of India could head it (asked in 2018). A change in **2019** opened the post to any **former Supreme Court Judge** and cut the term from five years to **three years, or till the age of 70**.

The President appoints the chairperson on the advice of a committee of six: the Prime Minister, the Speaker, the Home Minister, the two Leaders of the Opposition and the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. In 2025 the paper slipped in the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha, who is not on it. The present chairperson is **Justice V. Ramasubramanian**.
keep: State PSC member: six years or 62. UPSC: six years or 65.
Appointed by the Governor, removed only by the President.
Joint State PSC: created by Parliament.
NHRC: 1993 Act; term three years or 70 since 2019.
NHRC head can be a former Chief Justice of India or a former Supreme Court Judge.

3. It was set up under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

books.name: British Rule and Freedom
books.sub: From a trading company to the night of freedom

stories.title: A trading company gets a kingdom
stories.teaser: Three battles in seven years, and then the taxman arrives.
body: In 1757 the East India Company was still a trader. By 1765 it was collecting the taxes of a land larger than England. Three battles did it.

At **Plassey (1757)** Robert Clive beat **Siraj-ud-Daulah**, the Nawab of Bengal, with the help of the traitor Mir Jafar. At **Wandiwash (1760)** Eyre Coote beat the French and ended their dream in India (asked in 2018). Then came the real test.

At **Buxar (1764)** three rulers joined hands: **Mir Qasim** of Bengal, **Shuja-ud-Daulah** of Awadh and the Mughal emperor **Shah Alam II**. **Hector Munro** beat all three. Siraj was not there. He had died seven years before. By the **Treaty of Allahabad (1765)** the emperor gave the Company the **Diwani**, the right to collect revenue in **Bengal, Bihar and Orissa**.
Now the Company needed a system to collect land tax. It tried three.

**Lord Cornwallis** brought the **Permanent Settlement in 1793** in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. The **zamindars became owners** of the land, and the tax was **fixed for ever**. That is why it is called permanent.

In Madras and Bombay, **Thomas Munro** and Alexander Read used the **Ryotwari** system (asked in 2025). The government took the tax straight from the farmer, the ryot. In the North-Western Provinces and Punjab, **Holt Mackenzie** brought the **Mahalwari** system in 1822, where the whole village (mahal) paid together.
High taxes and cheap British cloth then broke India’s old crafts. Historians call this **deindustrialisation** (asked in 2021).
keep: Buxar 1764: Munro beat Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah and Shah Alam II.
Treaty of Allahabad 1765: Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
Permanent Settlement: Cornwallis, 1793, zamindars, revenue fixed for ever.
Ryotwari: Munro, Madras and Bombay. Mahalwari: Holt Mackenzie, 1822.

asked.q:
Consider the following statements about the Permanent Settlement:
1. It was introduced by Lord Cornwallis in 1793.
2. It made the zamindars the owners of the land.
3. Under it, the land revenue was revised every thirty years.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Which of the following was NOT part of the alliance defeated by the British at the Battle of Buxar (1764)?

stories.title: The ladder of Acts
stories.teaser: Each Act of the British Parliament added one rung. Climb it once and you can place any of them.
body: British rule in India was built by Acts of Parliament, one rung at a time. Climb the ladder once.

**1773, Regulating Act.** The first rung. It made **Warren Hastings** the Governor-General of Bengal and set up a Supreme Court at Calcutta, with **Elijah Impey** as its first Chief Justice. **1784, Pitt’s India Act.** A **Board of Control** in London now watched the Company.

**1813, Charter Act.** The Company lost its trade monopoly, and **₹1 lakh a year** was set aside for education (asked in 2021). **1833, Charter Act.** The Governor-General of Bengal became the **Governor-General of India**; William Bentinck was the first. A Law Member joined his council, and that was **Macaulay** (asked in 2025).

**1853, Charter Act.** The Company could no longer hand out civil service jobs to friends. Posts were thrown open to **competition**. The Macaulay Committee of 1854 planned the exam, and in 1863 **Satyendranath Tagore** became the first Indian to pass it.

**1858, Government of India Act.** After the Revolt, the Crown took over. A new minister, the **Secretary of State for India**, sat in London with a council of 15. The Governor-General got a second title, **Viceroy**; **Lord Canning** was the first.

**1861** brought Indians into the law-making council. **1892** made a small start with elections (asked in 2018). **1909**, the Morley–Minto reforms, gave separate electorates to Muslims. **1919**, the Montagu–Chelmsford reforms, brought **dyarchy** to the provinces. **1935** gave **provincial autonomy** and a **federal court** (asked in 2025) and separated Burma from India.
keep: 1853: open competition for the civil service.
1858: Secretary of State for India; Viceroy (Canning first).
1833: Governor-General of India; Macaulay first Law Member.
1813: one lakh rupees for education.
1919: dyarchy in provinces. 1935: provincial autonomy, federal court.

stories.title: Two viceroys and a classroom
stories.teaser: Lytton shut mouths, Ripon opened doors, and both left exam questions behind.
body: Two Viceroys ruled one after the other and could not have been more different.

**Lord Lytton (1876–80)** held a grand **Delhi Durbar in 1877** to declare Queen Victoria the Empress of India, while a famine was killing people in the south. In **1878** he passed the **Vernacular Press Act** to silence Indian-language newspapers, and the **Arms Act**, which stopped Indians from keeping weapons without a licence.

**Lord Ripon (1880–84)** undid much of it. He **repealed the Vernacular Press Act in 1882**. He passed the **first Factory Act in 1881**. His **Resolution of 1882** set up local boards with elected members, and for this he is called the **Father of Local Self-Government**. His law member wrote the **Ilbert Bill (1883)**, which would have let Indian judges try Europeans. The white community’s anger over that Bill has been asked in 2018 and 2025.
Ripon also set up the **Hunter Education Commission (1882)**. That takes us to the classroom.

The story of English education has one famous paper. In **1854 Charles Wood** sent a despatch asking for schools at every level, from the village to the university. It is called the **Magna Carta of English Education in India**. The universities of **Calcutta, Bombay and Madras** opened three years later, in 1857. Before it stood **Macaulay’s Minute of 1835**, which chose English as the language of teaching.

After Wood came a line of commissions, and the 2025 paper asked their order: **Hunter (1882), Raleigh (1902), Sadler (1917), Hartog (1929), the Wardha scheme (1937), Sargent (1944), Radhakrishnan (1948), Kothari (1964)**.
keep: Ripon: Father of Local Self-Government (Resolution of 1882).
Ripon also: first Factory Act 1881, repeal of Vernacular Press Act 1882, Ilbert Bill 1883.
Lytton: Delhi Durbar 1877, Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act 1878.
Wood’s Despatch 1854: Magna Carta of English Education.
Order: Hunter, Raleigh, Sadler, Hartog, Wardha, Sargent, Radhakrishnan, Kothari.

asked.q: Who is called the 'Father of Local Self-Government' in India?
Which document is known as the 'Magna Carta of English Education in India'?

stories.title: Before the Congress, the printing press
stories.teaser: Small clubs and brave newspapers came first. The Congress came later.
body: The Congress was born in 1885, but it had many elder brothers. Educated Indians first met in small clubs in the big cities.

In **1863 Abdul Latif** started the **Mohammedan Literary Society** in Calcutta. In **1866 Dadabhai Naoroji** started the **East India Association** in London to tell the British public about India. In **1870 M. G. Ranade** and his friends started the **Poona Sarvajanik Sabha**. In **1876 Surendranath Banerjea** and Ananda Mohan Bose started the **Indian Association**, the strongest of them all. A year or two later **Syed Amir Ali** founded the **Central National Mohammedan Association** (asked in 2025). The Madras Mahajan Sabha (1884) and the Bombay Presidency Association (1885) came just before the Congress.
These men needed a voice, and the voice was the newspaper. Learn each paper with its owner.

**Raja Rammohan Roy** ran Sambad Kaumudi. **Dadabhai Naoroji** ran Rast Goftar. **G. Subramania Iyer** founded The Hindu. **Sisir Kumar Ghosh** founded Amrita Bazar Patrika. **Tilak** ran Kesari and Mahratta. **Annie Besant** ran New India and Commonweal. **Maulana Azad** ran Al-Hilal. **Maulana Mohammad Ali** ran **Comrade**, and the examiner likes to swap these last two. **Gandhi** ran Young India and Harijan. **Ambedkar** ran Mook Nayak.
Odisha has two names to keep. **Utkal Dipika (1866)** of **Gourishankar Ray** was the first Odia newspaper. **The Samaja (1919)** was started by **Gopabandhu Das**.

The rulers hit back with press laws. **Wellesley** brought censorship in **1799** (asked in 2025). **John Adam** made licences compulsory in 1823. **Charles Metcalfe** removed the curbs in 1835 and is called the liberator of the Indian press. India’s first newspaper was Hicky’s Bengal Gazette (1780).
keep: Indian Association 1876: Surendranath Banerjea.
Poona Sarvajanik Sabha 1870: M. G. Ranade. East India Association 1866: Dadabhai Naoroji.
Mohammedan Literary Society 1863: Abdul Latif.
Comrade: Mohammad Ali. Al-Hilal: Azad.
Utkal Dipika: Gourishankar Ray. The Samaja: Gopabandhu Das.

stories.title: The man they blamed for the unrest
stories.teaser: A British journalist gave Tilak an insult. India kept it as a title.
body: In 1910 a British journalist named **Valentine Chirol** wrote a book called “Indian Unrest”. He wanted to find who was to blame for the anger in India, and he pointed at one man. He called **Bal Gangadhar Tilak** the **Father of Indian Unrest**. Tilak took him to court in London and lost. But the insult became a medal.

Tilak had earned it. He ran two newspapers, **Kesari** in Marathi and **Mahratta** in English. He turned the Ganapati and Shivaji festivals into public meetings. He gave the country a line it still remembers: **“Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it.”**

He was one of three leaders called **Lal–Bal–Pal**. They were the Extremists, who wanted to fight and not just to request. At **Surat in 1907** the Congress split between them and the Moderates. The British sent Tilak to **Mandalay** jail in Burma for six years, and there he wrote the Gita Rahasya. He came back, started a **Home Rule League in 1916**, and helped join the Congress and the Muslim League in the **Lucknow Pact** the same year.

“Lal” was **Lala Lajpat Rai**, the **Punjab Kesari**. He founded the newspaper **The Punjabee** and the Servants of the People Society, and he was the first president of the All India Trade Union Congress in 1920. He died in 1928 after a police lathi charge during the protest against the Simon Commission. The 2025 paper had a statement question on him.
“Pal” was **Bipin Chandra Pal** of Bengal, who edited New India and Bande Mataram. If the examiner has done Lal, then Bal and Pal are due.
keep: Valentine Chirol called Tilak the Father of Indian Unrest.
Tilak: Kesari, Mahratta, Home Rule League 1916, Mandalay jail.
Lajpat Rai: Punjab Kesari, The Punjabee, first AITUC president, died 1928.
Surat split 1907. Lucknow Pact 1916.

asked.q: Who called Bal Gangadhar Tilak the 'Father of Indian Unrest'?

stories.title: Four fights, then Karachi
stories.teaser: Gandhi tested his method in four small struggles before he used it on the whole country.
body: Gandhi came home from South Africa on 9 January 1915. He did not jump into national politics. He tested his method, satyagraha, in four small fights, and their order is a ready-made exam question.

First came **Champaran (1917)** in Bihar, for farmers forced to grow indigo. Second came the **Ahmedabad Mill Strike (early 1918)**, where he went on his **first hunger strike** for the workers’ wages. Third came **Kheda (1918)** in Gujarat, where farmers refused to pay tax after their crops failed. Fourth came the **Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919)**, his first all-India call, against a law that allowed jail without trial. It ended in the blood of **Jallianwala Bagh** on 13 April 1919.

After that the fights were national, and the 2018 paper asked their order too: **Non-Cooperation (1920)**, the **boycott of the Simon Commission (1928)**, **Civil Disobedience (1930)** and **Quit India (1942)**.

In between, the Congress sessions tell the story. At **Belgaum (1924)** Gandhi presided, the only time he ever did (asked in 2018). At **Lahore (1929)** Jawaharlal Nehru presided and the goal became Purna Swaraj; the first Independence Day was kept on **26 January 1930** (asked in 2025). Gandhi broke the salt law at Dandi on **6 April 1930** (asked in 2018).

Then came **Karachi, March 1931**. Bhagat Singh had been hanged only days before, and the mood was dark. **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel** presided. The session approved the Gandhi–Irwin Pact and passed the famous resolution on **Fundamental Rights and the National Economic Programme**. The 2025 paper said Motilal Nehru presided. That was the trap.
Later sessions: **Faizpur (1936)** was the first held in a village. At **Tripuri (1939)** Subhas Bose beat Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
keep: Order: Champaran 1917, Ahmedabad 1918, Kheda 1918, Rowlatt 1919.
Karachi 1931: Sardar Patel presided; Fundamental Rights resolution.
Belgaum 1924: the only session under Gandhi.
Lahore 1929: Nehru, Purna Swaraj. Faizpur 1936: first village session.

stories.title: Red flags in the mills
stories.teaser: The 2025 paper asked four questions on labour and the Left. This is their story.
body: After the First World War, prices rose and wages did not. Workers in the mills of Bombay, Calcutta and Ahmedabad began to strike, and leaders came forward to organise them.

In **1920** the **All India Trade Union Congress** was born in Bombay. **Lala Lajpat Rai** was its first president, and **N. M. Joshi** was one of its builders (asked in 2025). In Ahmedabad, **Gandhi** founded the Textile Labour Association (asked in 2018).

A new idea was also arriving from Russia. **M. N. Roy** founded the **Communist Party of India** at Tashkent in 1920 (asked in 2025). In Bengal in **1925** a small group formed the **Labour Swaraj Party**. Its leaders were **Muzaffar Ahmed**, the poet **Qazi Nazrul Islam** and **Hemanta Kumar Sarkar**. The 2025 paper asked about this party twice, and its trap was **S. A. Dange**, who belonged to Bombay and not to this party.

The government was frightened. In **1924** it tried Dange, Muzaffar Ahmed and others in the **Kanpur Bolshevik Conspiracy Case**. Then, in **March 1929**, it arrested about thirty labour leaders in one sweep, among them **Muzaffar Ahmed, S. A. Dange and P. C. Joshi**, along with three Englishmen. The trial was held far from the mill cities, in a small town. This was the **Meerut Conspiracy Case (1929–33)**.

The case failed in its aim. It made the accused famous, and Nehru himself helped their defence. In **1934** Jayaprakash Narayan and Acharya Narendra Dev formed the **Congress Socialist Party** inside the Congress. In **1936** the **All India Kisan Sabha** met at Lucknow under Swami Sahajanand Saraswati.
Do not mix up the cases. **Kakori (1925)** was a train robbery by revolutionaries. The **Lahore** case was against Bhagat Singh. **Alipore (1908)** was against Aurobindo Ghosh.
keep: Meerut Conspiracy Case 1929: Muzaffar Ahmed, Dange, P. C. Joshi.
Labour Swaraj Party 1925: Muzaffar Ahmed, Nazrul Islam, Hemanta Sarkar (not Dange).
AITUC 1920: Lajpat Rai first president; N. M. Joshi.
CPI: M. N. Roy. Congress Socialist Party: 1934.

stories.title: An army born in a prison camp
stories.teaser: The Indian National Army had a founder before Netaji.
body: In February 1942 Singapore fell to Japan, and thousands of Indian soldiers of the British army became prisoners. One of them, **Captain Mohan Singh**, asked a bold question: why not turn these prisoners into an army to free India? With Japanese help he raised the **first Indian National Army in 1942**.

The political side was led by an old revolutionary living in Japan, **Rash Behari Bose**, who headed the **Indian Independence League**. But Mohan Singh soon quarrelled with the Japanese, and the first INA broke up.

Then the man it needed arrived. **Subhas Chandra Bose** had slipped out of his house in Calcutta in 1941, reached Germany, and in 1943 travelled by submarine to the East. Rash Behari Bose handed the movement to him.

On **21 October 1943**, in **Singapore**, Netaji announced the **Provisional Government of Free India** (asked in 2018). He gave the army its cries, “Delhi Chalo” and “Jai Hind”, and a women’s unit, the **Rani of Jhansi Regiment**, led by Lakshmi Sahgal. The INA fought on the Burma border and reached Imphal and Kohima before the tide turned.

The war ended, and the British made a mistake. In **1945** they put three INA officers on trial at the **Red Fort**: **Shah Nawaz Khan, P. K. Sehgal and G. S. Dhillon**. The whole country rose in their support. **Bhulabhai Desai** led the defence, and Nehru put on his lawyer’s gown after many years.
Other fights from abroad have been asked too: the **Ghadar Party** at **San Francisco** (2018) and Savarkar’s **Free India Society** in London (2021).
keep: First INA: Captain Mohan Singh, 1942.
Indian Independence League: Rash Behari Bose.
Provisional Government: Subhas Bose, Singapore, 21 October 1943.
Red Fort trials 1945: Shah Nawaz Khan, Sehgal, Dhillon; defended by Bhulabhai Desai.

stories.title: Four new chairs
stories.teaser: In 2026 every top post in the armed forces got a new name on the door.
body: The year 2026 was unusual for the forces. All four of the top chairs changed hands within five months. The 2021 paper asked “the present Chief of Air Staff”, so this is a question waiting to happen.

On **31 May 2026** two men took over on the same day. **General N. S. Raja Subramani** became the **third Chief of Defence Staff**, after Bipin Rawat and Anil Chauhan. **Admiral Krishna Swaminathan** became Chief of the Naval Staff, after Admiral Dinesh K. Tripathi. On **30 June 2026 General Dhiraj Seth** became Chief of the Army Staff, after General Upendra Dwivedi. On **31 October 2026 Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit** became Chief of the Air Staff, after A. P. Singh.
The Chief of Defence Staff is the newest of these posts. It was created in 2019 so that the three forces plan and fight together. The main job of the new CDS is to set up joint **theatre commands**.

Now the ranks, which the 2021 paper also asked. The three forces use different names for the same level, and one word is a trap. A **Captain in the Navy is equal to a Colonel in the Army**. He is far senior to an Army Captain.

Go up the ladder with three names on each step, Army, Navy, Air Force. **Major, Lieutenant Commander, Squadron Leader. Lieutenant Colonel, Commander, Wing Commander. Colonel, Captain, Group Captain. Brigadier, Commodore, Air Commodore. Major General, Rear Admiral, Air Vice Marshal. Lieutenant General, Vice Admiral, Air Marshal. General, Admiral, Air Chief Marshal.**
Above them all sit three honorary ranks: Field Marshal, Admiral of the Fleet and Marshal of the Air Force. Arjan Singh is the only officer ever made Marshal of the Air Force.
keep: CDS (3rd): General N. S. Raja Subramani, 31 May 2026.
Army: Dhiraj Seth. Navy: Krishna Swaminathan. Air: Ashutosh Dixit.
Navy Captain = Army Colonel = Group Captain.
Squadron Leader = Major. Commodore = Brigadier.

asked.q: Who took over as India's third Chief of Defence Staff on 31 May 2026?
A Captain in the Indian Navy is equal in rank to a ____ in the Indian Army.

stories.title: The exercise calendar
stories.teaser: Each exercise has a partner country. The examiner swaps the partners.
body: Every year the forces train with friendly countries, and each exercise has a fixed name. The exam has asked **Dharma Guardian** with **Japan** twice, in 2021 and 2025. Its seventh edition was held in **Uttarakhand** in 2026.

The Army’s exercises are the largest group. **Yudh Abhyas** is with the USA. **Shakti** is with France. **Nomadic Elephant** is with Mongolia (asked in 2025). **AUSTRAHIND** is with Australia. **Surya Kiran** is with Nepal, **Sampriti** with Bangladesh and **Mitra Shakti** with Sri Lanka. **Garuda Shakti** is a special forces exercise with **Indonesia**.

Then comes the trap: three Central Asian neighbours with names that sound alike. **KHANJAR** is with **Kyrgyzstan**; in 2026 it was held at Misamari in Assam. **DUSTLIK** is with **Uzbekistan**; in 2026 it was at Aundh, Pune. **KAZIND** is with **Kazakhstan**. Say them three times.

At sea, **Malabar** began in **1992** between India and the USA. **Japan** became a permanent member in 2015 and **Australia** joined in 2020. So it has four members, the same four as the **Quad** (asked in 2021). France is not one of them; India’s naval exercise with **France is Varuna**. With Japan alone it is JIMEX, with Singapore SIMBEX and with the United Kingdom Konkan.

Do not confuse these with **MILAN**. MILAN is not with one country. It is a **multilateral** meeting of many navies, hosted by the Indian Navy every two years. It began in **1995** in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and later moved to **Visakhapatnam**, the home of the Eastern Naval Command. In **February 2026** MILAN and the **International Fleet Review** were held there ⟨CHECK⟩. The Navy’s own biggest drill is **TROPEX** (asked in 2025).
keep: KHANJAR: Kyrgyzstan. DUSTLIK: Uzbekistan. KAZIND: Kazakhstan.
Dharma Guardian: Japan. Nomadic Elephant: Mongolia. Garuda Shakti: Indonesia.
Malabar: India, USA, Japan, Australia. Varuna: France.
MILAN: multilateral, hosted by the Indian Navy at Visakhapatnam.

stories.title: The missile family
stories.teaser: Know each missile by where it starts and what it hits.
body: In 2025 the paper said Pralay was an air-to-surface cruise missile and asked if that was correct. It was not. The examiner changes one word in the description, so you must know each missile by two things: where it is fired from and what it hits.

Start with the **Agni** family. They are **surface-to-surface ballistic missiles**, fired from land at targets on land, and they rise high before falling. **Agni-5** is the longest, with a range of **more than 5,000 km**. **Prithvi** is the short-range member of the same kind. **Pralay** is also surface-to-surface. It is called quasi-ballistic because it can change its path in flight, and its range is only about **150 to 500 km**.

**BrahMos** is different. It is a **cruise missile**, which flies low like a plane without a pilot. It is **supersonic**, faster than sound, and it was built by **India and Russia** together. Its name joins two rivers, the **Brahmaputra and the Moskva**. **Nirbhay** is India’s slower, subsonic cruise missile.

**Akash** is a **surface-to-air** missile: it is fired from the ground at enemy aircraft. **Astra** is **air-to-air**, fired from one aircraft at another. **Nag** is an **anti-tank** missile. The **S-400** air defence system was bought from **Russia** (asked in 2021).

Many of these came from one programme, the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme, led by Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam. **Dr Tessy Thomas**, who led the Agni projects, is called the Missile Woman of India (asked in 2021).

Most tests happen on the Odisha coast: the **Integrated Test Range at Chandipur** and **Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam Island**. A **scramjet** engine, asked in 2025, burns fuel in air moving faster than sound and has no moving parts.
keep: Agni-5: surface-to-surface ballistic, over 5,000 km.
BrahMos: supersonic cruise missile, India and Russia.
Akash: surface-to-air. Astra: air-to-air. Nag: anti-tank.
Pralay: surface-to-surface, quasi-ballistic, short range.

asked.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Agni-5 is a surface-to-surface ballistic missile with a range of more than 5,000 km.
2. BrahMos is a subsonic cruise missile developed by India and Israel.
3. Akash is a surface-to-air missile.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

stories.title: Who guards which border
stories.teaser: Six forces, six jobs, and one ministry that is not the Ministry of Defence.
body: The soldier you see at a border post is often not from the Army. He belongs to one of the **Central Armed Police Forces**, and all of them work under the **Ministry of Home Affairs**, not the Ministry of Defence. This one fact is the examiner’s favourite false statement.

Each force was born from an event. After the war with China in 1962, India raised the **Indo-Tibetan Border Police** to watch the **China** border (the 2025 paper had three statements on it). The **Sashastra Seema Bal** followed in 1963 and now guards the open borders with **Nepal and Bhutan**.

After the war with Pakistan in 1965, India raised the **Border Security Force** on **1 December 1965**. The BSF guards the borders with **Pakistan and Bangladesh**. The link with Bangladesh also explains “Operation Zero Line” in the 2025 paper.

The oldest force of all is the **Assam Rifles**, raised in **1835**. It guards the border with **Myanmar**. The **Central Reserve Police Force** began in **1939** and handles trouble inside the country. The **Central Industrial Security Force**, raised in **1969**, protects airports, the Delhi Metro and big industries. The **National Security Guard**, the black cat commandos, came in 1984.
One force breaks the rule. The **Indian Coast Guard**, set up in **1978**, is under the **Ministry of Defence**. It runs SAREX, the national sea rescue exercise, which was held off Paradip in 2026.
keep: BSF: raised 1965; Pakistan and Bangladesh borders; Home Ministry.
ITBP: 1962, China. SSB: Nepal and Bhutan. Assam Rifles: 1835, Myanmar.
CISF 1969, CRPF 1939.
Coast Guard is under the Ministry of Defence.

asked.q:
Consider the following statements about the Border Security Force (BSF):
1. It was raised in 1965.
2. It guards India's borders with Pakistan and Bangladesh.
3. It works under the Ministry of Defence.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

stories.title: Where officers are made, and how they are honoured
stories.teaser: A map of the training academies, and the two ladders of medals.
body: A young cadet’s road begins near Pune. The **National Defence Academy** is at **Khadakwasla, Pune**, and trains cadets of all three forces together. After that the roads part.

Army cadets go to the **Indian Military Academy at Dehradun**. Navy cadets go to the **Indian Naval Academy at Ezhimala** in Kerala. Air Force cadets go to the **Air Force Academy at Dundigal** near Hyderabad. Those who join the Army for a short service go to the **Officers Training Academy at Chennai**; a second one is at Gaya. The examiner likes to place the OTA in Pune, because the NDA is there.

Senior officers return to study. The **Defence Services Staff College** is at **Wellington** in the Nilgiris. The **College of Defence Management** is at Secunderabad. The **National Defence College** is in New Delhi. The **Indian National Defence University** is coming up at **Binola in Haryana**, and that one has been asked twice (2018 and 2021). The police have their own academy, the **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel National Police Academy at Hyderabad** (asked in 2025).
Now the medals. There are two ladders, and each has three steps.
For bravery **in war**: the **Param Vir Chakra**, then the Maha Vir Chakra, then the Vir Chakra. For bravery **in peacetime**: the **Ashoka Chakra**, then the Kirti Chakra, then the Shaurya Chakra.

The first Param Vir Chakra went to **Major Somnath Sharma** in 1947. The only Air Force officer to get it is **Flying Officer Nirmal Jit Singh Sekhon**, for the 1971 war (asked in 2021). The medal itself was designed by Savitri Khanolkar.
keep: OTA: Chennai (and Gaya). NDA: Khadakwasla, Pune.
IMA: Dehradun. Naval Academy: Ezhimala. Air Force Academy: Dundigal.
Indian National Defence University: Binola, Haryana.
Highest in peacetime: Ashoka Chakra. Highest in war: Param Vir Chakra.

stories.title: An operation needs a name
stories.teaser: The 2025 paper asked three operation names. Here are the ones since then.
body: When the forces go out to fight or to help, the mission gets a name. The 2025 paper asked three: **Operation Jindagi** (the rescue at the Silkyara tunnel), **Operation Keller** (against terrorists in Shopian) and **Operation Olivia** (the Coast Guard’s watch over nesting olive ridley turtles in Odisha).
The year 2025 gave four more, and they tell a story of a busy year.
On **28 March 2025** a great earthquake hit **Myanmar**. India sent rescue teams, a field hospital and ships within hours. This was **Operation Brahma**.

On **22 April 2025** terrorists killed tourists at **Pahalgam** in Kashmir. On **7 May 2025** India struck terror camps across the border. This was **Operation Sindoor**. A later operation that hunted down the Pahalgam attackers was named Operation Mahadev.
In **June 2025** fighting broke out between Israel and Iran, and thousands of Indian students were stuck. India brought them home in **Operation Sindhu**.
In late **2025 Cyclone Ditwah** flooded **Sri Lanka**. India sent ships and aircraft with relief. This was **Operation Sagar Bandhu**, “friend across the sea”.
In **2026** came **Operation Urja Suraksha**. “Urja” means energy. When the Strait of Hormuz crisis put oil and gas ships in danger, the **Navy escorted** them to India.
Notice the pattern. Most of these are not about fighting. They are about rescue and relief, and the examiner likes exactly these.
keep: Brahma: earthquake relief to Myanmar, 2025.
Sindoor: strikes after the Pahalgam attack, 7 May 2025.
Sindhu: bringing Indians home from Iran, 2025.
Sagar Bandhu: cyclone relief to Sri Lanka, 2025.
Urja Suraksha: Navy escorts for oil and gas ships, 2026.

stories.title: The words of ecology
stories.teaser: A handful of scientists gave ecology its vocabulary. Every paper asks one of their words.
body: Every ASO paper has asked the meaning of some word from ecology: plankton in 2018, hemiparasites in 2021, edge species and endemic species in 2025. The words become easy when you meet the people who made them.

**Ernst Haeckel** coined the word **ecology**, the study of living things and their surroundings. **A. G. Tansley** coined **ecosystem** in 1935. **Charles Elton** drew the first **pyramid of numbers**: many plants at the bottom, fewer plant-eaters, very few hunters at the top.

Why does the pyramid narrow? **Raymond Lindeman** answered in 1942 with the **10 per cent law**. Only about **10%** of the energy at one level passes to the next. The rest is lost as heat. So a pyramid of **energy is always upright**; it can never stand on its tip.

Next, how do you measure the richness of life? **R. H. Whittaker** gave three measures. **Alpha diversity** is the variety inside one community, such as one pond. **Beta diversity** is the **change in species as you move from one community to the next**, say from the pond to the forest beside it. **Gamma diversity** is the total over the whole region (asked in 2021).

Where two communities meet there is a border zone called an **ecotone**. Species that live mainly in that zone are **edge species** (asked in 2025). A species found in only one region of the world is **endemic** (asked in 2025).

That brings us to **Norman Myers**. In 1988 he gave the idea of the **biodiversity hotspot** (asked in 2021). A region must pass two tests: it must have at least **1,500 endemic plant species**, and it must have **lost at least 70%** of its original vegetation. The world has **36** hotspots. **Four** touch India: the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, the Western Ghats with Sri Lanka, and Sundaland, which includes the Nicobar Islands.
keep: 10 per cent law: Raymond Lindeman, 1942.
Beta diversity: change between communities. Gamma: the whole region.
Hotspot: 1,500 endemic plants and 70% of vegetation lost. Idea of Norman Myers.
Ecosystem: Tansley. Ecology: Haeckel. Pyramid of numbers: Elton.

stories.title: A town, a poison, a promise
stories.teaser: Most environment treaties are named after the town where they were signed.
body: Environment treaties are easy to mix up, because each is known by a town’s name. Tie each town to one problem.

Begin in **Stockholm**, twice. In **1972** the first big UN meeting on the environment was held there; World Environment Day, 5 June, marks its opening. In **2001** the **Stockholm Convention** was signed, and it deals with **persistent organic pollutants**. These are poisons such as DDT that do not break down and travel up the food chain.

**Minamata** is a town in Japan where factory waste poisoned the sea. The Minamata Convention deals with **mercury** (asked in 2021). **Basel** controls the movement of hazardous waste between countries. **Rotterdam** says dangerous chemicals can be traded only with the buyer’s informed consent. **Ramsar**, a town in Iran, gave its name to the wetlands treaty of 1971. **CITES**, signed in Washington, controls trade in endangered animals and plants. **Montreal (1987)** protects the ozone layer.
Now the climate story, which has its own line of towns.

At the **Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 1992**, countries signed the **UN Framework Convention on Climate Change**. The same summit gave the Convention on Biological Diversity and Agenda 21. Rio also gave the rule of **common but differentiated responsibilities** (asked in 2021): all must act, but rich countries, who polluted first, must do more.

The countries then meet every year in a “COP”. At **Kyoto**, on **11 December 1997**, they adopted the Kyoto Protocol (asked in 2025), which came into force in 2005 and named six greenhouse gases. At **Paris in 2015**, COP21, they agreed to hold warming well below 2°C. COP30 was at **Belém, Brazil** in 2025, and COP31 at **Antalya, Türkiye** in 2026.
keep: Stockholm Convention 2001: persistent organic pollutants.
Minamata: mercury. Basel: hazardous waste. Ramsar: wetlands. Montreal: ozone.
UNFCCC: Rio Earth Summit, 1992.
Kyoto Protocol adopted 11 December 1997. Paris Agreement 2015.

stories.title: Counting trees and tigers
stories.teaser: India counts its forests every two years and its tigers every four.
body: Every two years the **Forest Survey of India** at **Dehradun** photographs the country from satellites and publishes the **India State of Forest Report**. The exam has used it twice, in 2018 and 2025.

The 2023 report has a few lines worth keeping. Forest and tree cover together make up **25.17%** of India. **Madhya Pradesh** has the **largest forest area**, followed by Arunachal Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. By share of its own land, **Lakshadweep** is first, and **Mizoram** is first among the States. The four States that added the most forest and tree cover were **Chhattisgarh, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha and Rajasthan**; that was the 2025 question, and Odisha is in it.

Tigers get their own count. **Project Tiger** began in **1973**. The count of 2022 found **3,682** tigers, and the next result is due in 2027. The list of tiger reserves keeps growing: the **56th** was Guru Ghasidas–Tamor Pingla in Chhattisgarh, the **57th** was Ratapani in Madhya Pradesh, and the **58th**, in **March 2025**, was **Madhav**, also in Madhya Pradesh. That State now has nine, the most in India. Odisha has two: Similipal and Satkosia.

Some parks are known for a single animal. **Kaziranga** in Assam means the **one-horned rhinoceros**. **Gir** in Gujarat holds every wild **Asiatic lion** on earth, 891 at the 2025 count. **Dachigam**, near Srinagar, protects the **hangul**, the Kashmir stag. **Keibul Lamjao** in Manipur floats on Loktak Lake and is the only home of the **sangai**, the brow-antlered deer. Manas in Assam was asked in 2018.
In Odisha, Bhitarkanika has saltwater crocodiles, Chilika has Irrawaddy dolphins and Similipal has black tigers.
keep: Largest forest area: Madhya Pradesh. Total forest and tree cover: 25.17%.
Top four in increase: Chhattisgarh, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha, Rajasthan.
58th tiger reserve: Madhav, Madhya Pradesh, March 2025.
Keibul Lamjao: sangai. Dachigam: hangul. Gir: lion. Kaziranga: rhino.

stories.title: The pollution watchers
stories.teaser: One board, born from a water law, now measures the air as well.
body: In 1974 Parliament passed a law to keep rivers clean, the **Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act**. To enforce it, the law created a new body, the **Central Pollution Control Board**. So the CPCB was **born from the Water Act in 1974**. Its duties over air came later, with the **Air Act of 1981**.

Then came a night that changed Indian law. In December 1984 gas leaked from a factory in **Bhopal** and killed thousands. Parliament answered with the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986**, a wide law that lets the Centre act on any kind of pollution.
Two more dates complete the set. The **Wild Life (Protection) Act** is older, from **1972**. The **National Green Tribunal**, a special court for environment cases, came in **2010**.

The CPCB’s daily work has already given two exam questions. Under the **National Air Quality Monitoring Programme** it measures pollutants at each station **twice a week** (asked in 2021). And it built the **Comprehensive Environmental Pollution Index**, a score for polluted industrial areas, together with **IIT Delhi** (asked in 2025).

It also runs the **Air Quality Index** you see in the news, which uses eight pollutants and six colour bands from Good to Severe. Under the **National Clean Air Programme**, cities must cut the dust called PM10 by up to 40%.
A few poison names travel with this topic. **Minamata disease** comes from mercury. **Itai-itai** comes from cadmium. **Blue baby syndrome** comes from nitrates in drinking water.
keep: CPCB: set up 1974 under the Water Act.
Air Act 1981. Environment (Protection) Act 1986, after Bhopal.
Wild Life Act 1972. National Green Tribunal 2010.
CEPI was made with IIT Delhi. Air monitoring is twice a week.

asked.q: The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) was set up in 1974 under the:
asked.a: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974

books.name: Economy and Planning
books.sub: Plans, deficits, prices and the poor

stories.title: Everyone had a plan
stories.teaser: Before India had a Planning Commission, four different groups had already written a plan.
body: In the 1940s freedom was close, and everybody asked the same question: how will a poor country grow? Four groups wrote four answers, and the exam can ask any of them.

In **1944** eight big businessmen, among them **J. R. D. Tata and G. D. Birla**, wrote the **Bombay Plan**. The same year **Shriman Narayan Agarwal** wrote the **Gandhian Plan**, built around villages and small industry. In **1945 M. N. Roy**, the old communist who appears in the labour story too, wrote the **People’s Plan**, which put farming and the needs of the poor first. In **1950 Jayaprakash Narayan** wrote the **Sarvodaya Plan**.

Then the government took over. The **Planning Commission** was set up on **15 March 1950** by a resolution of the Cabinet, and the Prime Minister was its chairman. The **First Plan (1951–56)** stressed farming. The **Second (1956–61)** followed **P. C. Mahalanobis** and built heavy industry.
Things did not always go to plan. After two wars and a drought, India ran three one-year plans from **1966 to 1969**, a gap known as the **Plan Holiday**.

Now the question this exam has asked three times. In **1978** the **Janata government of Morarji Desai** ended the Fifth Plan early and tried a new idea, the **Rolling Plan**. Each year the targets and the money were looked at again and the plan was “rolled” one year forward. The idea came from the economist **Gunnar Myrdal**. It lasted only till 1980 and was **not part of any Five Year Plan**. The paper asked what it means (2018), who adopted it (2021) and which Plan introduced it, where the answer was “none of the above” (2025).
Planning ended on **1 January 2015**, when **NITI Aayog** replaced the Commission. “Economic and social planning” sits in the **Concurrent List** (asked in 2021).
keep: People’s Plan 1945: M. N. Roy. Gandhian Plan: S. N. Agarwal.
Bombay Plan 1944: industrialists. Sarvodaya Plan 1950: Jayaprakash Narayan.
Rolling Plan: 1978–80, Morarji Desai, idea of Gunnar Myrdal, not in any Five Year Plan.
Planning Commission: 15 March 1950. NITI Aayog: 1 January 2015.

asked.q: The 'People's Plan' (1945) for the economic development of India was prepared by:

stories.title: The four gaps
stories.teaser: A budget has four kinds of gap. Each is the one before it with something taken out.
body: A government, like a family, can spend more than it earns. The budget measures that gap in four ways. Learn them as a chain.

The **revenue deficit** is the simplest. It is the gap between the government’s day-to-day spending and its day-to-day income. The **fiscal deficit** is the total gap: all spending minus all income other than loans. In plain words, it is **what the government must borrow this year**. Budget 2026-27 aims at a fiscal deficit of **4.3% of GDP**.
Much of each year’s borrowing only pays interest on old loans. Remove that and you get the **primary deficit**: **fiscal deficit minus interest payments**.

The fourth is the newest, from the Budget of 2011-12. The Centre gives grants to the States, and part of that money builds lasting things such as roads and schools. It seems unfair to count that as wasteful spending. So the **effective revenue deficit** is the **revenue deficit minus grants given to States for creating capital assets**.
In 2025 the paper listed these four and added a fake fifth, “Monetary Deficit”. There is no such deficit in the budget.

Where does the States’ own money come from? Every five years the President sets up a **Finance Commission** under **Article 280**. It has **a chairman and four other members** (asked in 2021), and it decides how central taxes are shared.

The 14th Commission gave the States **42%**. The 15th cut it to **41%** after Jammu and Kashmir became a Union Territory. The **16th Commission**, under **Arvind Panagariya**, covers **2026 to 2031** and **kept 41%**. The law that keeps the deficits in check is the FRBM Act, reviewed by the N. K. Singh committee.
keep: Effective revenue deficit = revenue deficit − grants to States for capital assets.
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments.
“Monetary deficit” is not a budget term.
Finance Commission: Article 280, chairman plus four members.
16th Finance Commission: Arvind Panagariya, 2026–31, States’ share 41%.

asked.q: Effective Revenue Deficit is equal to the revenue deficit minus:
asked.a: grants given to States for creating capital assets

stories.title: Who watches prices, who counts growth
stories.teaser: The RBI has one target, the statistics office has one base year, and both changed their yardsticks in 2026.
body: Two numbers rule the economic news: how fast prices are rising, and how fast the economy is growing. Each has a keeper.

Prices first. Since 2016 the **Reserve Bank of India** has had one clear target: keep inflation at **4%**, with a band of **2% on either side**. So anything from 2% to 6% is allowed. The target is fixed by the **Government after talking to the RBI**. It is measured by the **Consumer Price Index**, the prices a family pays in the shop, and not by the Wholesale Price Index.

Who makes these indexes? The **CPI** comes from the **National Statistics Office**. The **WPI** comes from the Office of the Economic Adviser in the commerce ministry. To hit the target, a **six-member Monetary Policy Committee** moves the **repo rate**, the rate at which the RBI lends to banks. This whole design came from the **Urjit Patel Committee**.

That is one of many committee names. The **Narasimham Committee** reformed **banking**. The **Malhotra Committee** reformed **insurance**. The **Tendulkar Committee** drew the **poverty line**, and **Rangarajan** redrew it. The **Pherwani Committee** proposed the **National Stock Exchange** (asked in 2025). The 2025 paper also asked what the RBI does **not** do: it does not regulate stock exchanges. **SEBI** does, and SEBI also regulates mutual funds (asked in 2018).

Now growth. GDP is always compared with a **base year**, a normal year whose prices are used as the yardstick. In **February 2026** the statistics office released a new GDP series and moved the base year from 2011-12 to **2022-23**. The CPI got a new base too, **2024**.
Whichever year you use, one fact holds: the **services sector** gives the largest share of India’s GDP (asked in 2025).
keep: RBI inflation target: 4%, plus or minus 2%, measured by CPI.
New GDP base year: 2022-23 (released February 2026). New CPI base: 2024.
Narasimham: banking. Malhotra: insurance. Tendulkar: poverty line. Urjit Patel: inflation targeting.
Pherwani: National Stock Exchange. SEBI regulates stock exchanges, not the RBI.

Consider the following statements:
1. The RBI's inflation target is 4 per cent, with a band of 2 per cent on either side.
2. This target is measured by the Wholesale Price Index (WPI).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
The new series of India's GDP, released in February 2026, uses which base year?

stories.title: Counting the poor, and giving them work
stories.teaser: Poverty is no longer measured by income alone, and the job guarantee has a new name.
body: For decades India counted the poor by one test: does a person spend less than a fixed amount a day? The Tendulkar and Rangarajan committees argued over where to draw that line.

Then the idea changed. A family may have some income and still be poor if the children are out of school and there is no toilet or clean water. So the UNDP and Oxford University built the **Multidimensional Poverty Index**. It looks at **three dimensions, health, education and standard of living**, each with equal weight.

The global index uses **10 indicators**. India’s own version, made by **NITI Aayog**, uses **12**. The two extra ones are **maternal health** and a **bank account**. The data comes from the **National Family Health Survey** (asked in 2025). The 2021 paper asked who is in charge of measuring poverty, and the answer was NITI Aayog. By this measure, about **24.82 crore** Indians left poverty between 2013-14 and 2022-23.
Measuring is one job. Helping is another, and the biggest help in villages has been a promise of work.

In **2005** Parliament passed **MGNREGA**, which promised every rural household **100 days** of paid work a year. In **December 2025** Parliament replaced it with a new law, the **Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act**, called **VB–G RAM G** for short. It raises the promise to **125 days**.
“Employment” and “Poverty Alleviation” are both written in the syllabus. A change this large, in the best-known scheme of all, is close to a certain question.
keep: National MPI: NITI Aayog, three dimensions, 12 indicators (global index: 10).
Data source: National Family Health Survey.
MGNREGA 2005: 100 days.
VB–G RAM G Act, December 2025: 125 days.

asked.q: The National Multidimensional Poverty Index of NITI Aayog measures poverty in three dimensions using how many indicators?
The Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, which replaced MGNREGA, promises a rural household how many days of wage work in a year?

books.sub: The service you are trying to join, and the bodies that watch it

stories.title: The steel frame
stories.teaser: The story of the civil service, from a Company clerk to a protected officer.
body: You are sitting this exam to enter the civil service, so its history is your own family history. The 2025 paper asked five questions around it.

In the Company’s days, a job in India was a gift. Directors in London handed posts to their nephews. The **Charter Act of 1853** ended that, and the **Macaulay Committee (1854)** designed an open exam. But the exam was held in London, so very few Indians could try.

Indians pressed for change, and four bodies answered, in this order. The **Aitchison Commission (1886)** split the service into Imperial, Provincial and Subordinate branches. The **Islington Commission (1912)** looked again. The **Lee Commission (1923)**, whose full name is the Royal Commission on the Superior Civil Services (asked in 2025), asked for a Public Service Commission in India. The first one opened in **1926**.
The British Prime Minister **Lloyd George** called this service the **steel frame** that held the empire together. After freedom, **Sardar Patel** kept the frame and gave it a new purpose.

The Constitution protects the officer in three Articles. **Article 309** lets the government make service rules. **Article 310** says an officer serves at the pleasure of the President or the Governor. Then **Article 311** limits that pleasure with two shields: an officer **cannot be dismissed by anyone lower than the authority that appointed him**, and **not without an inquiry** where he can defend himself. **Article 312** lets Parliament create a new All India Service after the Rajya Sabha asks for it by a two-thirds vote (asked in 2021 and 2025).

New IAS officers train at the **Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration** at **Mussoorie**, set up in **1959**. It works under the **Department of Personnel and Training**, not the Home Ministry. The police academy at Hyderabad is the one under the Home Ministry.
keep: Order: Macaulay 1854, Aitchison 1886, Islington 1912, Lee 1923.
First Public Service Commission: 1926, after the Lee Commission.
Article 311: no dismissal by a lower authority, and not without an inquiry.
LBSNAA: Mussoorie, 1959, under the Department of Personnel and Training.
“Steel frame”: Lloyd George.

asked.q:
Arrange the following in the order in which they were set up (earliest first):
1. Lee Commission
2. Aitchison Commission
3. Macaulay Committee
4. Islington Commission
Which of the following statements about the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA) is NOT correct?
asked.a: It works under the Ministry of Home Affairs

asked.q: Which Article of the Constitution says that a civil servant cannot be dismissed by an authority lower than the one that appointed him, and not without an inquiry?

stories.title: The citizen at the counter
stories.teaser: Sevottam, the Citizen’s Charter and the websites that replaced the queue.
body: Picture a man at a government counter. He does not know how long his work will take, whom to complain to, or whether anyone will listen. A set of reforms tried to answer those three questions.
The first answer came from Britain in **1991**: the **Citizen’s Charter**. An office writes down, in public, what service it gives and in how many days. India adopted the idea in **1997**.

A charter on the wall is not enough. So in **2006** the **Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances** built a full model named **Sevottam**, from “seva” and “uttam”, excellent service. The 2025 paper asked what it is: a **quality management system** for public services. It has exactly **three modules**: the **Citizen’s Charter**, a **Public Grievance Redress** system, and **Service Delivery Capability**. Nothing in it is about staff pay.
The same department runs **CPGRAMS**, the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System. Any citizen can **lodge a complaint online** against any central office and track it.

Other websites took over other queues. **RTI Online** takes information requests. **GeM** is where government offices buy goods. **iGOT Karmayogi** trains officials. **DigiLocker** keeps your certificates. **UMANG** puts many services in one app. **PRAGATI** is the Prime Minister’s own screen for reviewing stuck projects.

Behind all of this stands the **Second Administrative Reforms Commission**. Its first report, “Right to Information: Master Key to Good Governance”, was asked in 2021. Its twelfth report was called “Citizen Centric Administration”. Odisha’s own step was **Mo Sarkar** in 2019, where officers phone citizens to ask how they were treated.
keep: Sevottam: three modules, Citizen’s Charter, Grievance Redress, Service Delivery Capability.
Sevottam is a quality management system, made by DARPG in 2006.
CPGRAMS: online public grievances.
Citizen’s Charter: UK 1991, India 1997.

asked.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three modules of the 'Sevottam' model?

stories.title: Catching the corrupt
stories.teaser: One committee in 1962 started a chain that ended with the Lokpal.
body: In **1962** the government asked **K. Santhanam** to study corruption in public life. His committee has now been asked twice: in 2021 and, for its year, in 2025. Almost every body that fights corruption today grew from its report.
Its first child was the **Central Vigilance Commission**, set up in **1964**. For decades it stood only on a government order. A law gave it **statutory status in 2003**.

The second idea took far longer. In **1963** the lawyer **L. M. Singhvi** coined the word **Lokpal**, a people’s guardian who could look into complaints against ministers. In 1966 the **First Administrative Reforms Commission**, led at first by Morarji Desai, asked for a Lokpal at the Centre and Lokayuktas in the States. Bill after bill failed for almost fifty years.

After the great public protest of 2011, Parliament passed the **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act in 2013**. It came into force in January 2014. The Lokpal has a **Chairperson and not more than eight Members**, and **half of them must be judicial Members**.

Can it look into the Prime Minister? **Yes**, but with limits. It cannot touch matters of foreign relations, security, public order, atomic energy and space. The first Chairperson was **Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose** in 2019. The present one is **Justice A. M. Khanwilkar**.

Beside these stands the citizen’s own tool, the **Right to Information Act, 2005**. An office must answer in **30 days**, or in **48 hours** if life or liberty is at stake. The 2018 paper asked about tools of accountability, and the 2021 paper said the strongest control by citizens is the **election**.
keep: Santhanam Committee: 1962. CVC: 1964, statutory in 2003.
Lokpal: word coined by L. M. Singhvi in 1963; Act of 2013.
Lokpal: Chairperson plus up to eight Members, half judicial; Prime Minister is covered with limits.
RTI: 30 days; 48 hours for life or liberty.

asked.q:
Consider the following statements about the Lokpal:
1. It has a Chairperson and not more than eight Members.
2. Half of the Members must be judicial Members.
3. The Prime Minister is fully outside its jurisdiction.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

stories.title: Four committees and a village
stories.teaser: It took thirty-five years and four committees to put the Panchayat into the Constitution.
body: Gandhi wanted every village to be a small republic. The Constitution only put that wish in **Article 40**, as a Directive Principle. Turning it into real power took four committees.

In **1957** the **Balwant Rai Mehta Committee** studied why village development schemes were failing. Its answer was that the people had no say. It proposed a **three-tier** system: the village panchayat, the block samiti and the district parishad. On 2 October 1959 Nehru opened the first of these at **Nagaur in Rajasthan**.
The new bodies soon grew weak, because State governments did not hold elections or give them money. In **1977** the **Ashok Mehta Committee** suggested a simpler **two-tier** system.

In **1985** the **G. V. K. Rao Committee** gave the sharpest line of all. Officials had taken over, it said, and Panchayati Raj had become **“grass without roots”**. It wanted the **district** to be the main unit of planning.
In **1986** the **L. M. Singhvi Committee**, led by the same man who coined “Lokpal”, said the only cure was to give Panchayats **constitutional status**, so that no State could ignore them.

That came with the **73rd Amendment of 1992**. It added Part IX and the **Eleventh Schedule** with **29 subjects**, made elections compulsory every five years, reserved **one-third of seats for women**, and created a State Election Commission and a State Finance Commission. The **74th Amendment** did the same for towns, with the Twelfth Schedule and 18 subjects.
One caution from 2025: the paper named the “B. R. Mehta Committee” among civil service committees. It does not belong there. It belongs here.
keep: Balwant Rai Mehta 1957: three-tier. First at Nagaur, Rajasthan, 1959.
Ashok Mehta 1977: two-tier.
G. V. K. Rao 1985: “grass without roots”; district as the unit of planning.
L. M. Singhvi 1986: constitutional status, which came with the 73rd Amendment.

asked.q:
Match List I (Committee) with List II (What it is known for):
List I: a. Balwant Rai Mehta Committee  b. Ashok Mehta Committee  c. G. V. K. Rao Committee  d. L. M. Singhvi Committee
List II: 1. Constitutional status for Panchayats  2. Three-tier Panchayati Raj  3. Two-tier Panchayati Raj  4. Called Panchayati Raj 'grass without roots'

books.name: Odisha
books.sub: Its rivers, hills, minerals, heroes and forests

stories.title: Six rivers, one coast
stories.teaser: Odisha’s coast was not always there. Six rivers built it, grain by grain.
body: Look at a map of Odisha’s coast, from Balasore down to Ganjam. Thousands of years ago much of that green strip was sea. Six rivers carried mud down from the hills and laid it at their mouths, and the six deltas slowly joined into one plain. Geographers call it the **Hexadeltaic region**, the land of six deltas. The 2025 paper asked why it has that name.

From north to south the six are the **Subarnarekha, Budhabalanga, Baitarani, Brahmani, Mahanadi and Rushikulya**. The **Mahanadi** did the most work, which was the 2021 question. One river that is **not** on the list is the **Indravati**. It rises in Kalahandi and turns its back on the coast, flowing west and south to join the Godavari.

Each of the six has a birthplace. The **Mahanadi** rises at Sihawa in Chhattisgarh. The **Baitarani** rises at Gonasika in Keonjhar. The **Budhabalanga** comes out of the Similipal hills. The **Rushikulya** rises in the Rushimala hills and is unusual because it has **no delta** at its mouth; that sandy mouth is where the olive ridley turtles nest.

The **Brahmani** has the best story. It has no single source. Two rivers come down from the Chota Nagpur plateau, the **Sankh** and the **Koel**, and they meet at **Vedavyas near Rourkela**. From that meeting point the river is called the Brahmani. The **Rengali Dam** stands on it further down. The 2021 paper matched the Rajgangpur–Panposh uplands with these same two rivers.
The Mahanadi’s helpers are the **Ib, Tel, Ong and Jira**. In the far south, the **Sabari and Sileru** of Malkangiri flow to the Godavari.
keep: Six delta rivers: Subarnarekha, Budhabalanga, Baitarani, Brahmani, Mahanadi, Rushikulya.
Indravati is not one of them; it joins the Godavari.
Brahmani = Sankh + Koel, meeting at Vedavyas near Rourkela.
Rushikulya has no delta. Baitarani rises at Gonasika.

asked.q: The coastal plain of Odisha is called the 'Hexadeltaic region' because it is built by the deltas of six rivers. Which of the following is NOT one of the six?
The Brahmani river is formed by the meeting of which two rivers at Vedavyas near Rourkela?

stories.title: Four hills and what lies under them
stories.teaser: The examiner asked the hills from north to south. The districts and the minerals come next.
body: In 2025 the paper named four hills of Odisha and asked for them in order from north to south. Take the same four and add the district of each, because that is the natural next question.

In the north-east stands **Meghasani**, “the seat of clouds”, in the **Similipal** hills of **Mayurbhanj**. In the middle of the State is **Malayagiri**, near Pallahara in **Angul**. In the west is **Gandhamardan**, on the border of **Bargarh and Balangir**, with the Nrusinghanath temple on one side and Harishankar on the other. In the south is **Mahendragiri**, in **Gajapati**, a hill of the Eastern Ghats tied to the story of Parashurama.
Higher than all of them is **Deomali** in **Koraput**, **1,672 metres**, the highest peak of Odisha.
Now dig under the hills. Odisha is one of India’s richest States in minerals, and the 2025 paper matched places with what is mined there.
**Bauxite**, the ore of aluminium, lies on flat hilltops. The biggest deposit is at **Panchpatmali in Koraput**, mined by **NALCO**, whose refinery is at Damanjodi. Gandhamardan has bauxite too.

**Chromite** comes from the **Sukinda valley in Jajpur** and from **Baula-Nuasahi in Keonjhar**. **Iron ore** comes from **Joda and Barbil in Keonjhar**, and from Gorumahisani and Badampahar in Mayurbhanj. **Coal** comes from **Talcher**, in the Brahmani valley, and from the Ib valley. The beach sands at **Chhatrapur in Ganjam** give **monazite**, a source of rare earths.
keep: Mahendragiri: Gajapati. Malayagiri: Angul. Meghasani: Mayurbhanj. Gandhamardan: Bargarh–Balangir.
Highest peak: Deomali, Koraput, 1,672 m.
Panchpatmali, Koraput: bauxite (NALCO).
Sukinda and Baula-Nuasahi: chromite. Joda–Barbil: iron ore. Talcher: coal. Chhatrapur: monazite.
